title: Asymptotic Analysis
body:
[[Time Complexity]]

The method behind the notation: describe how an [[Algorithm]]'s cost grows as $n \to \infty$
and ignore everything that stops mattering at that limit. It is analysis of the *asymptote*,
the shape of the curve far out, not of any particular run on any particular machine.

Two things get discarded, and both discards are deliberate:

- **Constant factors.** $3n$ and $n$ are both $O(n)$. A constant is a property of the
  hardware and the compiler, not of the algorithm, and next year's machine changes it.
- **Lower-order terms.** $n^2 + 100n + 5000$ is $O(n^2)$. For small $n$ the $100n$ dominates,
  but small $n$ is the case where nothing matters anyway.

What is left is the thing that survives every implementation of the algorithm, which is why
this is the vocabulary the rest of the degree uses.

## The three bounds

| Notation | Meaning | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| $O(f)$ | upper bound | grows no faster than $f$ |
| $\Omega(f)$ | lower bound | grows at least as fast as $f$ |
| $\Theta(f)$ | both | grows exactly like $f$ |

Formally, $T(n)$ is $O(f(n))$ when there are constants $c > 0$ and $n_0$ such that
$T(n) \le c \cdot f(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$. The "for all $n \ge n_0$" is the asymptotic
part: behaviour below $n_0$ is allowed to be anything at all.

Note that $O$ is only an upper bound, so an $O(n)$ algorithm is technically also $O(n^2)$.
True, useless, and the reason $\Theta$ exists. In practice people write $O$ and mean the
tight bound.

## The limitation

Asymptotic analysis says nothing about the constants, and constants decide real
performance at real input sizes. [[Insertion Sort]] is $O(n^2)$ and still beats
[[Merge Sort]] on 15 elements. It is a tool for choosing between *shapes* of algorithm, not
for predicting a runtime.

- [[Limit]] in [[CALCULUS 1]]: "as $n \to \infty$" is the same operation calculus takes, and
  $O$, $\Omega$, $\Theta$ are statements about $\lim T(n)/f(n)$ being bounded, bounded below, or
  finite and non-zero. The difference is that CS states it with an explicit $c$ and $n_0$ because
  it needs the bound to hold at finite input sizes
